The second ritual, Akal Bodhon ('the untimely awakening'), gives Bengal's autumnal puja its origin story. The Devi is traditionally worshipped in spring (Basant Panchami onwards); when Lord Rama needed her blessings before his battle with Ravana, Brahma advised him to awaken the sleeping Goddess — the gods rest during the sun's six-month southward journey — in the 'wrong' season of Ashwin. Rama's out-of-season invocation was so powerful that it established Sharadiya Durga Puja, the autumnal puja that has been celebrated every year since. Performed in the evening, the Bodhon is followed by three days of intense worship: Maha Saptami (Nabapatrika and prana-pratishtha), Maha Ashtami (Sandhi Puja), and Maha Navami, concluding with immersion on Dashami.

steps: Kalparambha (Ceremonial Beginning): Install a sacred earthen pot (ghata) filled with Ganga water, mango leaves, and coconut, and gather the twigs of auspicious trees — Asvattha (sacred fig), Bata (banyan), Asoka, and jackfruit — that will be used over the coming days

Sankalpa (Sacred Resolve): The family head or priest formally resolves to perform the Durga Puja authentically for the next three days (Maha Saptami, Maha Ashtami, and Maha Navami), naming the day, tithi, and purpose of the vrata

Bilva Nimantran (Inviting the Bilva): The Bilva (bael) tree is worshipped and the Goddess is invoked into it with red flowers, vermilion, water, and mantra — the tree becomes her seat for the duration of the puja
Akal Bodhon (Untimely Awakening): In the evening, the Goddess is ceremonially awakened out of season, commemorating Rama's invocation of Durga before his battle with Ravana
Amantran (Formal Invitation): The Goddess is respectfully invited to accept the puja and take her place in the home or pandal, after which the main three-day rites may begin
rituals.mantra:
सर्वमङ्गलमाङ्गल्ये शिवे सर्वार्थसाधिके । शरण्ये त्र्यम्बके गौरि नारायणि नमोऽस्तुते ॥ 

(Sarva-mangala-mangalye shive sarvartha-sadhike, sharanye tryambake gauri Narayani namostute)

purpose.description: Maha Saptami — the first great day of worship: Navapatrika (Kolabou) snan, Mahasnan, and Prana Pratishtha awaken the Goddess in her nine-plant form
purpose.addtional_description:
Maha Saptami opens the principal days of Durga Puja. Its central rite is the Navapatrika — literally 'nine leaves' — in which nine plants, each embodying a form of the Goddess, are bundled together with the Bilva branch invoked the previous evening. At dawn, before sunrise, the bundle is carried to a river or other water body and given its ceremonial bath (Kolabou snan). It is then draped in a red-bordered sari, adorned as a bride, and installed on a wooden seat to the right of Durga's image. In popular Bengali custom the Kolabou is affectionately treated as Ganesha's bride, though scripturally the nine plants together represent the Goddess herself in nine forms.

The puja proper begins with Mahasnan — a mirror is placed on a platter so that Durga's reflection is caught in it, and it is the reflection that is bathed with sacred materials: water, milk, ghee, honey, and other offerings. Next comes Prana Pratishtha, the ritual invocation of divine presence into the idol and the Navapatrika, after which the Goddess is worshipped with the full Shodashopachara — the sixteen traditional offerings from asana (seat) and padya (water for the feet) through arati and pushpanjali. Devotees gather through the morning for anjali, offering flowers at the Goddess's feet, and many keep a fast until the offerings are made.

steps: Navapatrika Snan (Kolabou Bath): Before sunrise, the bundle of nine plants — banana (kadali), kachu (arum), turmeric, Bilva, barley, pomegranate, Asoka, manaka, and paddy — is carried to a river or water body and ceremonially bathed
Sringara and Installation: The bathed Navapatrika is draped in a red-bordered sari, adorned like a bride, and installed on a wooden seat to the right of Durga's image
Mahasnan (Great Bath): A mirror is placed on a platter so the Goddess's reflection appears in it; the reflection — not the idol — is then bathed with water, milk, ghee, honey, and sacred materials
Prana Pratishtha: Divine presence is ritually invoked into the idol and the Navapatrika, consecrating them as the living form of the Goddess

Shodashopachara Puja: The full sixteen-step worship — seat, water, bath, clothes, ornaments, flowers, incense, lamp, food, betel, and arati — continues through the day, with devotees offering anjali (flowers) at the Goddess's feet
rituals.mantra:
या देवी सर्वभूतेषु शक्तिरूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥ 

(Ya devi sarvabhuteshu shakti-rupena samsthita, namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namah — salutation to the Devi who dwells in all beings as power, repeated three times before each offering)

purpose.description: Maha Ashtami — the most potent day of Durga Puja: the nine forms of the Goddess are worshipped, young girls are honoured as the living Devi, and Sandhi Puja marks the moment she slew the demons Chanda and Munda
purpose.addtional_description:
Maha Ashtami is the most intense day of Durga Puja. Nine small pots (nava-kalasha) are installed and the nine forms of the Goddess are invoked into them, and the day's puja is offered to all nine together — it is Durga's own day at the height of her power. Alongside the ritual worship, Kumari Puja is performed: young unmarried girls, classically nine of them aged two to ten, are seated, bathed, decorated with vermilion and new clothes, and worshipped as the living embodiment of the Goddess — the belief being that the Devi manifests most purely in the girl child. Families offer them food, gifts, and dakshina with full reverence.

Sandhi Puja — the 'juncture' worship — is the climax of the entire festival and falls within Maha Ashtami. It occupies the last 24 minutes of Ashtami tithi and the first 24 minutes of Navami tithi: a 48-minute window when the Goddess is worshipped in her fierce form as Chamunda. According to the Devi Mahatmya, it was at this very juncture that the Devi sprang from the brows of the warring goddesses and slew the demons Chanda and Munda. Because the window is fixed by the tithi, not the clock, it can fall at any hour — midnight observances are common. During Sandhi Puja, 108 lamps are lit and 108 lotuses offered, and the moment is considered the most auspicious of the whole puja.

steps: Mahasnan and Nava-kalasha Puja: The ritual bath is given and nine small pots are installed, invoking the nine forms of the Goddess into them; all nine are worshipped together through the day
Pushpanjali: Devotees offer flowers at the Goddess's feet in rounds with mantra — morning, midday, and a final round before Sandhi Puja — many fasting until the flowers are offered
Kumari Puja: Young unmarried girls are seated as the living Goddess, their feet washed, vermilion applied, and new clothes, food, and gifts offered to them with full ritual honour

Sandhi Puja: At the 48-minute juncture where Ashtami tithi ends and Navami begins, the Goddess is worshipped as Chamunda with 108 lamps, 108 lotuses, red hibiscus flowers, and the beating of drums — the fiercest and most auspicious moment of the festival
rituals.mantra:
कात्यायनाय विद्महे कन्याकुमारीं धीमहि तन्नो दुर्गाः प्रचोदयात् ॥ 

(Katyayanaya vidmahe kanya-kumarim dhimahi, tanno Durgah prachodayat — the Durga Gayatri, the principal mantra of Durgashtami worship)
rituals.fasting: Many devotees observe a complete fast on Maha Ashtami, taking food and water only after the morning pushpanjali; some hold it through the day until the evening's Sandhi Puja offerings are made

purpose.description: The worship of young unmarried girls as living embodiments of Goddess Durga, performed on Maha Ashtami
purpose.addtional_description:
Kumari Puja — also known as Kanya Puja, Kumarika Puja, or Kanjak Puja — is the worship of a young unmarried girl as the living Goddess. The philosophy behind it is that the Devi's power resides in its purest, unmanifest form in the kumari, the girl child who is yet to enter worldly life: she is not a symbol of the Goddess but, for the duration of the ritual, her presence. In Bengal the rite is performed on Maha Ashtami, most commonly with a single girl, though some panchayats worship nine, each representing a stage of the Goddess — Kumari, Trimurti, Kalyani, Rohini, Kali, Chandika, Shambhavi, Durga, and Subhadra — classically aged two to ten. A young boy is worshipped alongside as Batuk Bhairava, her guard.

The tradition was made famous far beyond Bengal by Sri Ramakrishna, who in 1883 worshipped a young Muslim girl as the Divine Mother with the full sixteen-step ritual, dissolving all distinctions of caste and creed in the act. In North India the same rite survives as Kanjak or Kanya Puja during Navratri, where girls are invited into homes, their feet washed, and halwa-puri-chana served to them before they are seen off with gifts and money. Across both traditions, the etiquette is the same: the girls are treated with the complete reverence owed to a deity, never scolded or hurried, and the family serves them before eating.

steps: Seating the Kumari: The girl — one, or nine aged two to ten — is seated on an asana and greeted with devotion; a boy is seated alongside as Batuk Bhairava
Padya and Sringara: Her feet are washed, and she is adorned with vermilion, alta on her hands and feet, flowers, sandalwood paste, and new clothes
Shodashopachara Puja: She is worshipped with the full sixteen offerings — seat, water, bath, clothes, ornaments, flowers, incense, lamp, and food — exactly as to an installed deity
Naivedya and Dakshina: She is served food — traditionally khichuri and labra with sweets in Bengal, halwa-puri-chana in Kanjak tradition — and given gifts and money
Pranama: The family bows and touches her feet, and sees her off with full honours; nothing she does during the puja is corrected or scolded
rituals.mantra:
या देवी सर्वभूतेषु बालरूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥ 

(Ya devi sarvabhuteshu bala-rupena samsthita, namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namah — salutation to the Devi who dwells in all beings in the form of a young girl)

purpose.description: Maha Navami — the last full day of Durga Puja, when the Goddess is worshipped as Mahishasuramardini, the annihilator of the buffalo demon
purpose.addtional_description:
Maha Navami is the ninth and final full day of worship. The day's puja begins with Mahasnan and the full Shodashopachara, and on this day the Goddess is worshipped in her aspect as Mahishasuramardini — she who slew the buffalo demon Mahishasura. According to the Devi Mahatmya, the Devi battled the demon through the days of the puja, and her victory is commemorated the following morning as Vijaya Dashami, the tenth day of triumph. Navami is thus the day of the Goddess at the very summit of her power, immediately before her departure.

The defining ritual of Maha Navami is the concluding Homa — the fire sacrifice offered into a consecrated pit with ghee, grains, and mantra, after which the three days of puja are ritually complete. The day is also famous for its bhog: the grandest of the festival, when khichuri, labra, and sweets are offered to the Goddess in vast quantities and then distributed as prasad; devotees commonly fast until the bhog has been offered. Where the Ashtami–Navami junction falls on Navami's side of midnight, the 48-minute Sandhi Puja to Chamunda is observed during Navami, and families who could not perform Kumari Puja on Ashtami do so today.

steps: Mahasnan and Shodashopachara Puja: The Goddess is given the ritual bath and worshipped with the full sixteen offerings, in her form as Mahishasuramardini, the slayer of the buffalo demon

Sandhi Puja (where the junction falls on Navami): The 48-minute worship of Chamunda at the Ashtami–Navami tithi junction, with 108 lamps and 108 lotuses, observed during Navami whenever the juncture falls on this side of midnight
Navami Homa: The concluding fire ritual — ghee, grains, and offerings are made into the consecrated fire with mantra, completing the three days of puja

Maha Bhog: The grandest food offering of the festival — khichuri, labra, fried vegetables, and sweets — is laid before the Goddess and then distributed to all as prasad, with devotees taking their own food only afterwards
Maha Aarti: The grand lamp-waving with conch shells, bells, and dhaak drums, after which devotees offer their final pushpanjali and pranam of the festival
rituals.mantra:
अयि गिरिनन्दिनि नन्दितमेदिनि 

(Ayi giri-nandini, nandita-medini — 'O daughter of the mountain, joy of the world': the opening of the Mahishasura Mardini Stotra)

purpose.description: Vijaya Dashami — the day of farewell: Devi Baran, Sindoor Khela, and the immersion (bisarjan) that closes Durga Puja
purpose.addtional_description:
Dashami is the tenth and final day of Durga Puja, the day of both victory and farewell. Vijaya Dashami commemorates the Goddess's triumph over Mahishasura, but in Bengal it is equally the emotional end of the festival — for here Durga is not only the fierce warrior but a daughter visiting her parental home, and her departure is bid with tears, vermilion, and the promise of return. In the evening the clay idols are immersed in rivers and water bodies, symbolising her return to her celestial abode after her days on Earth.

Before the immersion comes the farewell to the Goddess herself. Married women perform Devi Baran — each sumangali offers bel leaves, paddy, and vermilion at the Goddess's feet and feeds her sweets as one would a departing daughter. Then follows the famous Sindoor Utsav (Sindoor Khela): the women first apply sindoor to Durga and her entourage, then to each other's faces and hair-partings, dressed in white-and-red, wishing each other long and blessed married life. The play of vermilion is the festival's most iconic image of Dashami.

The immersion procession then carries the idols to the water with dhaak drums, conch shells, cymbals, and the cry that echoes through every Bengali neighbourhood — Aschhe bochhor abar hobe, 'it will happen again next year'. In the evening begins Bijoya: the young touch the feet of their elders, embraces (kolakuli) and sweets are exchanged, and the greeting 'Shubho Bijoya' carries the festival's warmth for days after the Goddess has gone.

steps: Devi Baran (Farewell Offering): Married women, dressed in white-and-red, offer bel leaves, paddy, and vermilion at the Goddess's feet and feed her sweets, as one bids farewell to a departing daughter
Sindoor Khela (Vermilion Play): The women apply sindoor to the Goddess and her family, then to each other's faces and hair-partings, wishing one another long and blessed married life
Darpan Bisarjan: The Goddess's reflection is shown in a mirror or vessel of water — the symbolic taking of leave before the physical immersion

Bisarjan (Immersion) Procession: The clay idols are carried in grand procession with dhaak drums, conch shells, cymbals, and devotional chants, to the cry of 'Aschhe bochhor abar hobe' — it will happen again next year
Bijoya Greetings: In the evening, the young touch elders' feet, kolakuli embraces and sweets are exchanged, and 'Shubho Bijoya' greetings carry the festival to its close
rituals.mantra:
या देवी सर्वभूतेषु शान्तिरूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥ 

(Ya devi sarvabhuteshu shanti-rupena samsthita, namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namah — salutation to the Devi who dwells in all beings as peace, the fitting farewell verse)

purpose.description: The tenth and final day of Sharad Navratri — victory of Rama over Ravana, of Durga over Mahishasura, and the triumph of good over evil
purpose.addtional_description:
Vijayadashami is the tenth and final day of Sharad Navratri, and both its names carry the same meaning: Vijayadashami from 'vijaya' (victory) and 'dashami' (tenth) — the day of victory — and Dussehra from the Sanskrit 'dasha-hara', the removal of ten, read both as Ravana's ten heads and as the ten vices the festival asks one to burn within oneself.

Its significance is twofold. In the Ramayana tradition of North India, this is the day Lord Rama defeated the ten-headed demon king Ravana who had abducted Sita — celebrated through nine nights of Ramlila theatre and the burning of towering effigies. In the eastern and southern traditions, it is the day Goddess Durga slew the buffalo demon Mahishasura after nine days of battle; in Bengal it is at once her day of victory and her day of farewell, when she is sent home with vermilion, tears, and the promise of return.

South India gives the day its own distinctive colour: the worship of the instruments of one's work and learning. Ayudha Puja honours tools, vehicles, machines and books as vessels of the divine; Vidyarambham initiates small children into learning, their first letters written in rice; and the Shami tree is worshipped — for it was on a Shami that the Pandavas hid their weapons during exile, retrieving them on this very day to begin their campaign of victory. Across all regions, Vijayadashami is counted among the most auspicious days of the year to begin any new venture.

steps: Ramlila Performances (North India): Nine days of dramatic enactment of the Ramayana reach their climax with Ravana's defeat
Ravana Dahan (North India): Giant effigies of Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Meghnad are burnt at dusk, to fireworks and cheering crowds, symbolising the destruction of evil
Aparajita Puja (North India): Worship of Aparajita, the invincible Goddess, for victory and success in one's undertakings
Ayudha Puja (South India): Tools, instruments, machines, vehicles and books are cleaned, decorated, and worshipped — honouring the divine in the implements of one's work
Vidyarambham / Aksharabhyasam (South India): Small children are initiated into learning, writing their first letters — traditionally 'Om' traced in a plate of rice grains
Shami Puja and Leaf Exchange (South and West India): The Shami tree is worshipped, recalling the Pandavas retrieving their hidden weapons on this day; its leaves are exchanged as gold
Devi Baran and Sindoor Khela (Bengal): Married women bid farewell to the Goddess with bel leaves, paddy and vermilion, and play sindoor with one another before her departure
Bisharjan (Bengal and East India): The clay idols of Durga are carried in grand procession with dhaak drums and immersed, closing Durga Puja with the cry of 'Aschhe bochhor abar hobe'

purpose.description: Kojagari Puja is one of the major festivals celebrated in West Bengal, Odisha and Assam. A special worship of Goddess Lakshmi is performed on this day
purpose.addtional_description:
Kojagori Puja (also spelled Kojagari or Kojagara) is the special worship of Goddess Lakshmi on the full-moon night of Ashwin — the Sharad Purnima — observed across West Bengal, Odisha and Assam. The name comes from the Sanskrit 'Ko jagarti?' — 'Who is awake?' — and holds the festival's whole belief: on this night Lakshmi descends to earth and wanders from house to house asking the question, blessing with wealth and prosperity only those she finds awake in devotion. To be found sleeping is to miss her visit for the year.

The Bengali observance begins at dusk, when courtyards and thresholds are decorated with alpona — patterns painted in white rice paste, including the Goddess's footprints walking into the house. Lakshmi is worshipped at night with paddy (dhan), lotus, coins and gold, sugarcane and sweets, accompanied by the owl, her mount. The signature offering is khiri — kheer or payesh — which is placed under the open sky: the full moon of Sharad Purnima is believed to drip amrita, nectar, into it, and the moon-blessed kheer is eaten as prasad the next morning.

Because the Goddess must find the household awake, families traditionally keep vigil through the night — playing cards, carrom or dice until dawn, a custom that has made Kojagari a night of indoor festivity as much as worship. In Odisha the same full moon is also celebrated as Kumar Purnima, when unmarried girls worship the moon for a good husband, and across North India the identical kheer-under-moonlight tradition marks Sharad Purnima — the year's most beautiful moon, celebrated wherever it is seen.

steps: Alpona: At dusk, courtyards and thresholds are painted with white rice-paste patterns — lotus motifs and the Goddess's footprints walking into the home
Lakshmi Puja: At night, the Goddess is worshipped with paddy (dhan), lotus, coins and gold, sugarcane, and sweets, with her owl mount beside her
Khiri Bhog: Kheer or payesh is offered to Lakshmi and then placed under the open full moon, believed to receive the moon's nectar overnight
Night Vigil: The family stays awake through the night — traditionally over games of cards, carrom, or dice — so that Lakshmi, asking 'Who is awake?', finds them alert
Morning Prasad: The moon-blessed kheer is distributed among family and neighbours as prasad
rituals.mantra:
नमस्तेऽस्तु महामाये श्रीपीठे सुरपूजिते । शङ्खचक्रगदाहस्ते महालक्ष्मि नमोऽस्तुते ॥ 

(Namastestu mahamaye shree-pithe sura-pujite, shankha-chakra-gada-haste Mahalakshmi namostute — salutation to Mahamaya, enthroned in abundance, holding conch, discus and mace)
rituals.fasting: Devotees observing the Kojagara vrat keep a day-long fast, taking food — traditionally the moon-blessed kheer — only after the night's Lakshmi Puja is complete

purpose.description: The fullest, brightest moon of the year — the night of Krishna's Maha Raas with the gopis, and of kheer set out to catch the moon's nectar
purpose.addtional_description:
Sharad Purnima is the full moon of the Ashwin month, and by common reckoning the most beautiful moon of the year: the monsoon has washed the skies clean, the moon is near the earth, and it is said to shine on this night with all sixteen of its kalas — its phases — complete. The night is traditionally called the Kaumudi celebration, the festival of moonlight, and the moon's rays are believed to be charged with amrita, nectar — a belief Ayurveda honours by prescribing moonlight exposure as healing.

It is also the night, says the Bhagavata tradition, of Krishna's Maha Raas: the night Krishna multiplied himself to dance with every gopi of Braj under the full moon in Vrindavan — which is why this full moon is also called Raas Purnima, and why night-long Raas Leela performances fill the temples of Vrindavan and Nathdwara on this date. In Gujarat the same moon is danced under as raas-garba; in Odisha it is Kumar Purnima, when unmarried girls worship the moon; and in Bengal it is Kojagori Lakshmi Puja, when the Goddess walks the earth asking 'Who is awake?' — one moon, many doors into the same night.

The best-known household observance is the kheer: rice cooked in milk and sugar, placed on the terrace or courtyard under the open moon for the night, so that the moon's nectar may fall upon it. It is eaten as prasad the next morning, and families gather through the night to keep it company — the quiet Indian tradition of simply being awake with a beautiful moon.

purpose.description: Auspicious fasting day dedicated to Lord Vishnu
purpose.addtional_description:
Ekadashi is the eleventh lunar day observed twice monthly (on Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha) dedicated to Lord Vishnu, considered one of the most meritorious fasts in Sanatana Dharma that purifies the mind, body, and soul while helping devotees gain control over their senses and overcome past sins.

The core rituals remain identical for both Shukla and Krishna Paksha Ekadashi, with the primary difference being that Shukla Paksha Ekadashi symbolizes growth and spiritual expansion, while Krishna Paksha Ekadashi focuses on introspection, renunciation, and inner purification.

steps: Sankalp (Vow Taking) Take a formal vow before Lord Vishnu by holding water in your right palm and stating your intention to observe the Ekadashi fast sincerely.
Morning Puja Worship Lord Vishnu with Tulsi leaves (most essential), yellow flowers, sandalwood paste, incense, and ghee lamps at the home altar.
Fasting Observance Observe the chosen fast type - Nirjala (no food/water), Phalahar (fruits/milk only), or Farali (sattvic foods) while completely avoiding grains, rice, pulses, onion, and garlic.
Katha Reading Listen to or recite the specific Ekadashi story associated with that particular tithi, as reading the katha is considered as important as the fast itself.

Parana (Breaking Fast) Break the fast on Dwadashi morning after sunrise by first offering food to Lord Vishnu, then feeding Brahmins or the needy, and finally consuming simple satvik food within the prescribed time window.
